p36-physics-pace.title: Pace, physics and mental load
p36-physics-pace.text: so in terms of delivery absolutely in terms of the pace probably not so much too fast yeah so but I mean you couldn't do it any way differently for a research study but if you're looking at four hours two hours to learn the platform yeah if you think so the biggest thing for us that is always hard to convey to decision makers is physics remains the sort of the bounding factor I've got to get from this point here to that point there and if the adversary can see me from 20k away then I'm doing that activity from 20k and if you're going at 3k an hour then that's going to take you a long time to get from here to over there so there's a level of um I think realism is not the right word that acceleration in terms of decision however on the flip side of it when the shit hits the fan you are probably going to be very frustrated as I move this thing to here I've now got to wait for this thing to get into place to go and do this thing here hurry up and get there but at the same time as a commander you're sat there thinking okay what am I going to do if this thing fails what am I then going to do what am I going to do so your mental load is still loaded it's just loaded in a slightly different way so you're always trying to balance cognitive capacity against the time pressure effectively
p36-physics-pace.prompt: so I would ask in your professional opinion obviously this is clearly we're trying to get at something that we think is of interest in this kind of setting and stuff in reality I'd imagine the strategic and tactical thing would probably be done by two people but how relevant would you say this kind of set up is
p36-physics-pace.speaker: participant
p36-physics-pace.context: Asked how relevant the set-up is to real operations.
p36-physics-pace.why: The simulation compresses time and distance; real operations are bounded by physics, so the load moves from deciding fast to waiting and contingency-planning.

refs.point: A busier queue did not push anyone onto the assistants. P36 puts the real pressure elsewhere: "physics remains the bounding factor", and the load becomes waiting and asking "what am I going to do if this thing fails". "Your mental load is still loaded it's just loaded in a slightly different way."

The time Suggest frees is spent elsewhere while a plan runs. P36 describes that dead time from the commander's side: "I've now got to wait for this thing to get into place", and uses it to plan for failure.
Others said the pace was unreal; P36 agrees ("in terms of the pace probably not so much") and says what sets the real pace: "if you're going at 3k an hour then that's going to take you a long time".

p36-lag.why: The real constraint is the lag between seeing a problem and being able to act on it, during which other problems arrive.

p36-resource-cascade.title: Over-allocate at the top and the shortage cascades down
p36-resource-cascade.text: horses the courses but I would argue that if you've not got the resources available to you at the low level then or you've over allocated resources at the high level then you're running out of resources cascade down so you're it's a balance it's never perfectly weighted one way or the other so if you're let's say you split the task this dude here is doing this task and all of a sudden has got no resource left look at the task I need more resource I told you need more resource when I told you this is my plan and this is I've got no redundancy here you're carrying risk whereas if you've done both it's your risk to carry on the flip side of it if you've over allocated a resource that's just wasted resource now I can't complete you might want more resource but I've got five tasks that I need to do so I'm balancing these five do what you can with what you've got let me know where it all falls down because it doesn't matter if yours falls down because yours is a moderate task I've got a critical one over here that I'm allocating more to

p36-resource-cascade.why: The two tiers are coupled through resources and risk; who carries the risk depends on who made the allocation.

refs.point: Handing over at one tier goes with handing over at the other (Suggest ×2.1 after a card, same person, same size). P36 explains the coupling: the top allocation sets the lower tier's risk ("I told you need more resource when I told you this is my plan ... you're carrying risk"). Their own card-then-Suggest gap was close to zero, so the link is the cohort's, not theirs.
Over-allocating at the top: "that's just wasted resource". In their own builds the cohort mostly trimmed the card's spare drone.

Operators overrode the cards to weigh other missions. P36 says it as a commander: "I've got five tasks that I need to do so I'm balancing these five", and "I've got a critical one over here that I'm allocating more to".

p36-in-on-loop.title: Human in the loop versus on the loop
p36-in-on-loop.text: a level of human to human trust presuming that in this instance it was human in the loop as in maybe human in the loop human on the loop I would say this I would say is human in the loop because you have to okay everything I'm still okaying the tasks that are out there whereas what you would want to do for a human on the loop would be just it just churns through I don't know conservative each time and you would set it up for for anything that's a critical you go for the aggressive or anything that's not you go for the conservative do all of that you start looking at it and go oh shit that's not right I need to send another one over here quickly or making that intervention at a timely point is challenging for on the loop there's got to be way more trust that it gets the answer right every time
p36-in-on-loop.speaker: participant
p36-in-on-loop.why: This set-up is human-in-the-loop (every task is okayed); on-the-loop would need rules set in advance and far more trust, because timely intervention is hard.

refs.point: The platform keeps the operator approving every allocation and plan. P36 calls that human-in-the-loop and spells out on-the-loop: a standing rule (Aggressive for critical missions, Conservative otherwise) that "just churns through", with intervention in time the hard part.

In the loop on paper, close to on the loop in practice: tactical plans get a median 2–4 s once Deploy unlocks and 468 of 486 consulted plans go out as they came. P36's line is about who approves; the data show how little approving can involve.
Much strategic work is deciding small missions before the cards arrive. P36's on-the-loop rule would hand exactly those decisions to a standing policy and keep the human for exceptions.

refs.point: Several operators asked for failure numbers. P36 wants them with context ("there's got to be something where it shows a bit of context to it"), because a bare "40% failure chance" reads as "no chance" when "the failure rate of doing nothing is 100%".

Operators facing random failures with no numbers felt they were deciding blind. P36 agrees the numbers should be shown ("great to see the information") and adds that people then need training to act on them: "there's always going to be a failure rate I'm just trying to make it as low as reasonable".
Lower-reliance operators attempted fewer recoveries. P36's rule cuts the other way: in search and rescue "you're always gambling with someone's life", so you act and "chip away at it".

p36-shared-risk.title: Decisiveness, stakes and not sharing the risk

p36-shared-risk.speaker: participant
p36-shared-risk.context: Told they were very decisive in play.
p36-shared-risk.why: Their speed came from planning experience and knowing it was a simulation; an inexperienced commander facing real casualties will be reckless or paralysed, and remote autonomy removes the shared risk that used to temper those decisions.

refs.point: "It's a game" was a common caveat. P36 says what changes with a life at stake ("I imagine you're going to see me less decisive if someone's gonna die at the end"), and that a commander who no longer shares the risk ("I might die alongside them") loses what used to temper the order.

Prior experience did not predict style here. P36 expects it to matter most when the stakes are real: their own "looking at a glance yes it's allocated what I needed ... cool let's start running with it" comes from experience, where a new platoon commander would be "foolhardy" or "almost paralysed". A game with no lives on the line hides that difference.

p36-staff-process.title: Trust in the process, not the answer
p36-staff-process.text: well it's kind of this how it works in military planning anyway so in a anything above probably not comfortable let's say a battle group level the battle group level of activity you have your staff planners so there's some really sorry I'm a lay person battle group level how do you say scale battle group would be your what you've described there is your strategic so looking at a level where I'm going to allocate team pockets of capability to go and do a specific task and there would be a staff there that would work up plans socialize those plans amongst themselves and back brief me as a commander I would then go okay yeah I want you a bit of that plan and a bit of that plan give me this new plan they'll go and write up by then sort of basically finish off that way so it's a it is always a collective input into it but I'm just getting the synthesis of them work because I can't as an individual I couldn't work through the ground the enemy the enemy's plan the likelihood of my plan succeeding the logistics behind it it would take me forever which is why you're sourcing that that work so at that level you're already in a position where somebody's just coming back to you with the answers as long as you have trust in how they've come up with those answers then you're going to and if it looks right because you've gone through the process yourself so as a you know by the time you become a battery commander you would have been a commander you would have been a staff officer you'd have worked up in those levels so you kind of understand how those answers are generated so there's a level of trust in that process
p36-staff-process.prompt: speaking specifically about the relationship between you and these two assistants these being autonomous systems yeah obviously that's not a million miles away from that being a human assistant who's helping you there that it's gonna be you and two people right do you have any feeling about the the difference there you spoke a lot about socializing socializing the decision-maker something like that how does that compare do you think to if you had two subordinate people here
p36-staff-process.speaker: mixed
p36-staff-process.context: Asked how the two assistants compare with two human subordinates; the researcher's aside ("sorry I'm a lay person ... how do you say scale") sits inside the cut.
p36-staff-process.why: Commanders accept staff answers because they have done those jobs themselves and trust how the answers were made — which an operator of an AI assistant has not.

refs.point: Plans are accepted after a brief look. P36 explains why that can be rational: answers from staff are taken "as long as you have trust in how they've come up with those answers", not re-derived.

Several operators wanted to know how the assistants decide. For P36 that is the basis of trust: a commander can take the staff's answers because "you'd have worked up in those levels so you kind of understand how those answers are generated". No operator has done the assistant's job.

The card pays where a job is too big to do quickly by hand. P36 gives the same reason for having staff at all: "I couldn't work through the ground the enemy, the enemy's plan, the likelihood of my plan succeeding, the logistics behind it it would take me forever which is why your staff do it".

p36-bad-plan-quickly.why: The specific danger of a confident assistant — a plan that looks right with a hole you have not worked through yourself, replicated to every commander at operational tempo.

refs.point: The tactical flaw was hidden and rarely seen. P36's central risk is that kind: a confident plan with "a massive hole in that plan that you're not seeing", replicated at pace.

P36 sees narrow context as normal ("you as a g2'er are will only see your part of the plan") and fine "as long as in each of them it's gone through the analytical process", and adds that this game's tasks are simple enough not to need more: a direct tension with those operators.
Operators wondered how the two assistants fit together. P36's model is staff cells that each see their part and first "come together" at the planning brief.

P11 wanted an assistant that checks their own plan. P36's checker tests the other agents' data instead, so a bad input shows up before the answers built on it.

"Give it a quick once over and go that looks about right ... whether or not it is right of course it's another question entirely": the brief check the timing data show, with its limit named.

P21 chained drones through each other's tasks for "redundancy for free". P36 does the same on simple missions ("every single drone is going to every single task so that if one of my drones fails ... my other drones are picking up the task"), which is why those plans need no checking afterwards.

In P36's account verifying happens around the plan, not in a long look at it: take it to the people who will carry it out ("go away and work out the plan") and keep it "open to challenge". Beside that sits "trust in the fact it's done the maths behind it and has allocated enough platforms", which is about all the cohort's 2–4 seconds of checking can cover.

Some operators want a human in the loop even one who cannot check. P36's check is not one person looking harder but a plan socialised so that "somebody is checking my thinking and has the option to challenge me".

Their claim that pressure made them verify less is the kind of claim the workload finding tests and does not support across people.
